topics.title: Unexpected Loss, UL Contribution and Economic Capital

selectors.name: UL contribution, identical loans
selectors.what: UL contribution of one loan in a portfolio of equal loans with one common correlation: ULC = UL x sqrt(rho), the plain form.

selectors.name: Single-asset unexpected loss
selectors.what: Standalone UL of one loan from exposure, PD, loss rate and their variances, with the binomial variance of default PD(1-PD). Includes computing the binomial variance or standard deviation of default on its own.

selectors.name: Portfolio UL for n identical loans
selectors.what: UL_p = UL x sqrt(n + rho(n^2 - n)), forward, or reverse-solved for n, rho or the single-loan UL.

selectors.name: Economic capital with the capital multiplier
selectors.what: EC = UL_p x CM for the portfolio, or ULC x CM for one loan; the answer that forgets the multiplier is the planted error.

selectors.name: Trap: standalone UL offered when the contribution is asked
selectors.what: The stem asks for a UL contribution or a portfolio figure and the single-asset UL (the intermediate result) sits among the options.

selectors.name: UL contribution in a general portfolio
selectors.what: UL contribution or portfolio UL where the loans are not identical: two or three assets with their own ULs and a correlation, or unequal sizes.
selectors.source: Vardeez: 'UL contributions (risk contributions)'; Map: 'UL for a single component in a portfolio'

topics.august: UL contribution straight forward numerical (identical loans).

maps.tested: The single most-corroborated topic in the entire dataset. Tested numerically far more often than conceptually. Two distinct question shapes recur: (i) compute UL for one asset from EL, PD, LGD/severity and the binomial variance of default, and (ii) compute the UL contribution of one asset inside a portfolio, which is the harder and more frequently reported version.
maps.specifics: Recall notes specify 'UL for a single component in a portfolio (numerical)' and 'Unexpected Loss Contribution: all loans with same value'. One source reports a candidate got economic capital wrong by omitting the capital multiplier. Closed-book formulas: UL = EAD x sqrt(PD x var(LGD) + LGD^2 x var(PD)); ULC = UL x sqrt(rho); UL_p = UL x sqrt(n + rho(n^2 - n)); EC = UL_p x CM. The intermediate-result trap is live here: GARP plants the single-asset UL as a distractor when ULC is asked.

topics.vardeez: Very Important. "Important Reading: unexpected loss calculations as well as risk contributions can show up."

topics.title: RAROC, Adjusted RAROC and Hurdle Rate

selectors.name: Compute RAROC
selectors.what: After-tax RAROC = (revenues - costs - expected loss - taxes + return on risk capital +/- transfers) / economic capital, in plain form or with inputs that do not belong (red herrings). Also the loan form of CR-5 g: loan revenues over capital at risk.

selectors.name: Find the hurdle rate
selectors.what: After-tax weighted cost of common equity (CAPM) and preferred equity at market values; then the accept or reject decision against it.

selectors.name: Adjusted RAROC
selectors.what: ARAROC = RAROC - beta x (market return - risk-free rate); accept if it exceeds the risk-free rate; the break-even beta.

selectors.name: Direction of the effect on RAROC
selectors.what: Which way RAROC moves when economic capital, income, expenses, expected loss, funding cost, tax or the confidence level change: a sensitivity question, not a plug-in.

selectors.name: Cost of capital from the break-even
selectors.what: Reverse-solves around the hurdle: the cost of common equity implied by a given hurdle or break-even, or the break-even revenue at which RAROC equals the hurdle.

selectors.name: Interpret and compare RAROC
selectors.what: Given RAROC figures for units, loans or projects, decide which adds value or ranks higher; EVA / NIACC positive exactly when RAROC is above the hurdle.
selectors.source: Vardeez: 'RAROC calculations' on ORR-18 c (calculate and interpret; compare business unit performance)

maps.tested: The rare heavily-computational topic inside Operational Risk. Three sub-questions recur: compute RAROC; compute adjusted RAROC (ARAROC); and compute the hurdle rate the RAROC must clear.
maps.specifics: Reported variants: '2 on adjusted RAROC'; 'effect on RAROC by changing its components (economic capital, income, expense)': a sensitivity/direction question, not a plug-in; 'find hurdle rate'; 'weighted cost of capital given break-even cost'. Hurdle rate = value-weighted cost of common equity (via CAPM) and preferred equity. The ARAROC adjustment is alpha minus (beta_E x excess market return). The polarity of each component's effect on RAROC is the corruption operator of choice.

topics.vardeez: ORR-18: Very Important. CR-5: "LO 23.g for RAROC is important, but RAROC is more important in Operational Risk".

topics.title: Volatility Smiles, Skews and Put-Call Parity

selectors.name: Equity skew: effect of strike and maturity
selectors.what: For equity options, how implied volatility changes with strike (it falls as the strike rises; low-strike options, deep out-of-the-money puts, carry the highest implied volatilities) and with maturity (the skew flattens as maturity increases; the term structure slopes up when short-dated volatilities are historically low and down when they are historically high). Plain form, no calculation.

selectors.name: Two questions on FX and equity smiles
selectors.what: Questions that put the FX smile and the equity smile side by side: which market shows which shape, which tails are heavy, and why.

selectors.name: Implied volatility shape for FX options
selectors.what: The FX smile is U-shaped: implied volatility is lowest at the money and rises progressively as the option moves into or out of the money, because the implied distribution has heavier tails than the lognormal and is more peaked. Deep out-of-the-money calls and puts are both priced relatively high.

selectors.name: Lognormal vols versus implied vols, FX and index
selectors.what: Comparing option prices from a single at-the-money lognormal volatility with market prices and implied volatilities: both FX wings and deep out-of-the-money index puts are priced below market, deep out-of-the-money index calls above market. Read the tails of the implied distribution against the lognormal with the same mean and standard deviation.

selectors.name: Equity options volatility smile property
selectors.what: The defining property of the equity smile: a downward-sloping skew, implied distribution with a heavier left tail and less heavy right tail than the lognormal, present since the October 1987 crash, with the reasons (leverage, volatility feedback, crashophobia).

selectors.name: Trap: FX explanation swapped with equities
selectors.what: The explanation or shape of one market is attributed to the other: FX is U-shaped with both tails heavy, explained by non-constant volatility and jumps; equity is skewed with a heavy left and thin right tail, explained by leverage, volatility feedback and crashophobia.

selectors.name: Put-call parity and one implied volatility
selectors.what: Put-call parity (p + S0 e^(-qT) = c + K e^(-rT)) needs no assumption about the price distribution, so a European call and put with the same strike and maturity have the same implied volatility and the smile is the same from either; it says nothing about equality across strikes. Also appears as a distractor in smile questions.

topics.august: Volatility skew 1Q - effect of changing maturity and strike (equity option).

maps.tested: Nine sources; both third-party sheets mark the chapter fully important with no LO carve-outs. Almost entirely qualitative. The discrimination is always between the equity smile (downward skew, fat left tail, crashophobia / leverage) and the FX smile (symmetric U-shape, fat both tails, stochastic volatility and jumps).
maps.specifics: Explicit recalls: '2 questions from volatility smiles on FX and equity options'; 'implied volatility: foreign exchange options shape'; 'lognormal vols vs implied vols for fx and index options'; 'equity options volatility smile property'. Also flagged: put-call parity's implication that a call and put at the same strike/maturity share one implied volatility (LO 17.b), reported as a standalone theory question. The sibling swap here is attributing the FX explanation to equities or vice versa.

maps.tested: Reported as a standalone theory item in one sitting.
maps.specifics: Reported: 'put call parity.' Within Part II its home is LO 17.b: the implication that a European call and put with the same strike and maturity must share one implied volatility, which is why the smile is measured identically from either. Do not treat this as a Part I recap; the exam tested it in its smile context.

topics.title: Fundamental Review of the Trading Book (FRTB)

selectors.name: Stressed ES 97.5% replaces 99% VaR
selectors.what: FRTB replaces the 10-day 99% VaR of Basel I and Basel 2.5 with stressed expected shortfall at 97.5%, based on how market variables moved in stressed conditions, and asks why. For normal losses 99% VaR = mu + 2.326 sigma and 97.5% ES = mu + 2.338 sigma, almost the same; for heavier tails 97.5% ES can be considerably greater than 99% VaR.

selectors.name: Liquidity horizons and the cascade ES
selectors.what: Liquidity horizons of 10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days (categories 1 to 5) assigned to risk factors by asset class, and the cascade ES = sqrt(ES1^2 + ES2^2 + 2 ES3^2 + 2 ES4^2 + 6 ES5^2), where ESj shocks only the categories j to 5 over overlapping 10-day stressed changes and the weights come from (LHj - LHj-1)/10 = 1, 1, 2, 2, 6.

selectors.name: Standardized vs internal models, desk tests
selectors.what: The two FRTB approaches: the standardized approach is always calculated and acts as a floor, internal models permission is granted desk by desk, and a desk drops to the standardized approach on failing the backtest (1-day VaR over 12 months: more than 12 exceptions at 99% or more than 30 at 97.5%) or the P&L attribution tests (Mean(U)/SD(V) within -10% to +10%, Var(U)/Var(V) below 20%, four or more breaches in 12 months).

selectors.name: Trading book / banking book boundary
selectors.what: How FRTB draws the line between the trading book (market risk capital) and the banking book (credit risk capital): intent to trade is no longer enough, the bank must be able to trade and manage the risks on a desk, assignment is at initiation, and transfers are allowed only in extraordinary circumstances with any capital benefit disallowed.

selectors.name: FRTB vs Basel I, II, 2.5: overall changes
selectors.what: Which change belongs to which accord: Basel I 1996 Amendment (10-day 99% VaR, multiplier m >= 3, backtest exceptions raise m), Basel II (IRB, operational risk, three pillars, market risk unchanged), Basel 2.5 (stressed VaR, incremental risk charge, comprehensive risk measure), and what FRTB changes against them (one stressed ES, liquidity horizons, desk-level approval, standardized floor, firmer book boundary).

selectors.name: Curvature risk charge
selectors.what: The standardized charge for gamma risk: shock factor i up and down by its risk weight Wi, take the delta-predicted change less the actual change in each direction, charge = max(Wi delta_i - dV+, -Wi delta_i - dV-, 0). Short options attract the charge; long options give zero.

maps.tested: Eight sources, and multiple recalls independently give the same count: 2-3 questions per sitting. Both third-party sheets mark the whole chapter important. Rising sharply in weight since 2021.
maps.specifics: Reported angles: the ES-replaces-VaR shift and why; liquidity horizons by asset class; the standardised approach vs. internal models approach; trading-book / banking-book boundary; and comparative questions framed as 'FRTB vs Basel 1, Basel 2, Basel 2.5: overall changes'. One source flags 'refer GARP for Curve Risk' specifically, i.e. the curvature risk charge is not well covered in condensed notes.

topics.vardeez: MR-18: Very Important, "Again Full chapter is IMP (Refer GARP for Curve Risk)". ORR-21: untiered in his sheet, but his theme "Basel III: three components and comparison with Basel I and II" draws on this reading. ORR-22: untiered (tier cell reads 0), but his themes "Stressed market VaR (calculations)" and "Basel 2.5 market risk calculation" land squarely here, so treat as high priority.

topics.title: Merton Model, Distance to Default and Risk-Neutral PD

selectors.name: Distance to default, then rating band
selectors.what: Compute the distance to default (full form DD = [ln(V0/D) + (r - sigma_V^2/2)T] / (sigma_V x sqrt(T)), equal to d2 when drift is r) and then assign a rating band from the score; also the KMV form of DD. A lower DD means default is more likely.

selectors.name: Back out V0 and sigma_V
selectors.what: Solve the two simultaneous equations for the asset value and asset volatility from equity value and equity volatility, using the solver's converged N(d1) and N(d2): V0 = [E0 + D e^(-rT) N(d2)] / N(d1) and sigma_V = sigma_E E0 / [N(d1) V0].

selectors.name: Risk-neutral versus real-world PD
selectors.what: Risk-neutral PD = N(-d2) with assets growing at r; the real-world PD replaces r by the expected asset return mu. Includes choosing which of the two to use (valuation versus scenario analysis) and which is larger.

selectors.name: Merton PD to average hazard rate
selectors.what: Convert the Merton cumulative PD Q(T) into an average hazard rate: lambda = -ln(1 - Q(T)) / T, not Q/T.

selectors.name: Leverage ratio to return on equity
selectors.what: Equity return from the asset return through the equity delta: change in E / E0 is about N(d1) x (V0/E0) x (change in V / V0); equivalently sigma_E = N(d1) x (V0/E0) x sigma_V.

selectors.name: Short-form DtD versus full form
selectors.what: Choose between the short form DtD = ln(V/F) / sigma_V, valid as an approximation for a one-year horizon with drift about 0, and the full form with r or mu and T, when the question gives the drift or asks for d2.

selectors.name: Trap: Merton cannot be used beyond one year
selectors.what: A statement that Merton or the distance to default applies only to a one-year horizon is a false absolute: DD is defined for default T years in the future, with drift scaling with T and volatility with sqrt(T), including two- and three-year horizons.

selectors.name: Equity as call, debt as put; Merton limitations
selectors.what: Conceptual questions on the Merton set-up: equity as a call option on the firm's assets (E_T = max(V_T - D, 0)) with shareholders as option buyers and creditors as writers, debt as risk-free debt less a put, the basic assumptions (one zero-coupon bond, default only at maturity, constant asset volatility, unobservable V0 and sigma_V) and the limitations or extensions that follow.

maps.tested: Named by GARP-facing sources as the most consistently tested individual topic. Appears both computationally (DtD, PD, implied V0 and sigma_V) and conceptually (equity-as-call, debt-as-put, assumptions and limitations). One recall reports three questions from Merton in a single sitting; another reports two.
maps.specifics: Specific variants reported: 'finding distance to default and assign a rating based on the score'; 'Merton model, calculation of V0 and sigma(V)' (the simultaneous-equation form); 'Merton model risk-neutral prob'; 'hazard rate and PD based on Merton model'; 'leverage ratio -> ROE'. The formula card carries both the full form and the short form DtD = ln(V/F)/sigma: the short form is the shortcut GARP rewards when drift is about 0. Watch the scope trap: 'Merton cannot be applied beyond one year' is a false absolute.

topics.title: CVA, DVA, BCVA and CVA as a Spread

selectors.name: BCVA as a spread
selectors.what: BCVA = -average EPE x Spread_C - average ENE x Spread_P, in the units of the spread, with no LGD and undiscounted exposures; with average EPE = -average ENE this is -EPE x (Spread_C - Spread_P).

selectors.name: UCVA from EPE profile and PDs
selectors.what: Unilateral CVA from an EPE profile and a PD term structure: UCVA = -LGD x sum over intervals of EPE(ti) x marginal PD(ti-1, ti), with LGD = 1 - R and the EPE discounted (with explicit discount factors, the sum of (1-RR) x EE x PD x DF).

selectors.name: CVA as a running spread
selectors.what: Converts CVA into a running spread: UCVA = -average EPE x credit spread (undiscounted EPE, no LGD, in the units of the spread), or upfront CVA divided by (notional x risky annuity).

selectors.name: BCVA = CVA + DVA, sign convention
selectors.what: Computes DVA from the ENE profile with the party's own PD and own LGD, then BCVA = CVA + DVA; CVA is negative (a cost) and DVA is positive because ENE is negative.

selectors.name: BCVA with survival adjustments
selectors.what: CVA = -LGD_C x sum of EPE(ti) x PD_C(ti-1, ti) x [1 - PD_P(0, ti-1)] and DVA = -LGD_P x sum of ENE(ti) x PD_P(ti-1, ti) x [1 - PD_C(0, ti-1)], then BCVA = CVA + DVA.

selectors.name: Trap: change from UCVA to BCVA
selectors.what: The stem asks for the change from UCVA to BCVA, which is BCVA - UCVA = DVA + (CVA - UCVA), the DVA benefit plus the small survival reduction of the CVA leg; the BCVA itself or the DVA leg alone sits among the options as the intermediate-result distractor.

selectors.name: Distinguish CVA, DVA and BCVA
selectors.what: A definitional question separating the adjustments: what each measures (CVA from EPE and the counterparty's default, DVA from ENE and one's own default, BCVA as their sum with survival terms), their signs, and how UCVA and UDVA differ from BCVA.
selectors.source: Map: 'a definitional-distinction audit between the three adjustments'

maps.tested: Described by one importance sheet as 'a favourite topic of GARP - you cannot afford to skip this chapter at all.' Tested as computation and as a definitional-distinction audit between the three adjustments.
maps.specifics: Reported: '2 numericals on BCVA, CVA (couldn't do them)'; 'UCVA as a spread - calculation (formula)', listed twice in the same consolidated sheet, so the spread form specifically is the tested one. Closed-book: UCVA = sum of (1-RR) x EE x PD x DF; UCVA spread = -EPE x credit spread; BCVA = CVA + DVA with survival adjustments and the sign convention CVA negative, DVA positive. Intermediate-result trap: BCVA planted as a distractor when the change from UCVA is asked.

topics.vardeez: CR-20: Very Important. "CVA/BCVA and DVA is a favorite topic of GARP. Know the formulas very well. You cannot afford to skip this chapter at all."

topics.title: Ho-Lee, Time-Dependent Drift and Volatility

selectors.name: Ho-Lee top node after two months
selectors.what: Interest rate after 2 months in the top node of a monthly Ho-Lee tree (dt = 1/12): r0 + (lambda1 + lambda2) x dt + 2 x sigma x sqrt(dt), the change from today being the drift sum plus two up moves.

selectors.name: August plain forms: Ho-Lee, drift, volatility
selectors.what: The two plain forms recalled from August 2026: a Ho-Lee numerical with plug-in values, and a theory question on time-dependent drift and time-dependent volatility.

selectors.name: Rate in upper nodes, Ho-Lee or Model 3
selectors.what: Value of the short rate in the upper nodes of a Ho-Lee tree (constant sigma) or of a time-dependent-volatility tree (Model 3, dr = lambda(t) dt + sigma(t) dw with sigma(t) = sigma x e^(-alpha t)), built step by step from the stated drifts and volatilities.

selectors.name: Ho-Lee and Model 3 two-step plug and play
selectors.what: Two-step calculation with given inputs: Ho-Lee upper node r0 + (lambda1 + lambda2) dt + 2 sigma sqrt(dt); Model 3 upper node r0 + (lambda1 + lambda2) dt + [sigma(t1) + sigma(t2)] sqrt(dt); and the two-step standard deviation sqrt(dt) x sqrt(sigma(t1)^2 + sigma(t2)^2).

selectors.name: No-arbitrage model, node-2 change and drift
selectors.what: Change in the short rate at node 2 of a Ho-Lee tree, (lambda1 + lambda2) dt + 2 sigma sqrt(dt) for the top node, and the drift and volatility read back from given nodes: lambda1 = [(ru + rd)/2 - r0] / dt and sigma = (ru - rd) / (2 sqrt(dt)). Includes the uses of arbitrage-free models and the fitting issue.

selectors.name: Two questions on the Ho-Lee short-rate tree
selectors.what: The 'two on interest rate term structure (Ho-Lee)' pair: node values on the monthly tree (date-1 nodes r0 + lambda1 dt +/- sigma sqrt(dt); date-2 nodes r0 + (lambda1 + lambda2) dt + {2, 0, -2} sigma sqrt(dt)) and a reverse-solve for the drift or the volatility from given nodes.

selectors.name: Sibling swap: Vasicek, Models 1 and 2
selectors.what: A question that sets Ho-Lee or time-dependent volatility beside its siblings: Model 1 (dr = sigma dw, no drift), Model 2 (dr = lambda dt + sigma dw, constant drift) and Vasicek (mean reversion), on drift, mean reversion, flat or humped volatility term structure, parallel shifts and negative rates.

topics.august: Ho-Lee numerical - plug values; time-dependent drift and vol - theory question.

maps.tested: One sheet writes 'calculations are super important here': this is one of the few places where the quantitative work is the whole question. Two-step binomial node construction is the dominant format.
maps.specifics: Highly specific recalls: 'calculate interest rate after 2 months in the top node in Ho-Lee model'; 'Ho Lee and time-dependent volatility models: calculate value of rate in upper nodes'; 'Ho Lee Model & Model 3, 2-step plug and play calculation'; 'no-arbitrage model (Node 2 delta r)'; '2 on IR term structure (Ho Lee)'. Node formula: r0 + sum of lambda x dt +/- m x sigma x sqrt(dt). Sibling swap risk against Vasicek and Model 1/2.

topics.title: Correlation Swaps, Quanto Options and Concentration Ratio

selectors.name: Correlation swap payoff, fixed-rate payer
selectors.what: Payoff to the fixed-rate payer (the correlation buyer) = N x (realised correlation - fixed correlation), where realised correlation is the simple average of the pairwise correlations (the i > j cells, 2/(n^2 - n) times their sum). Example: pairs 0.5, 0.3, 0.1 give 0.3; fixed 10%, notional USD 1,000,000, payer receives USD 200,000.

selectors.name: Correlation swap payoff, seller's side
selectors.what: The same swap from the fixed-rate receiver (the correlation seller): payoff = N x (fixed correlation - realised correlation), with volatilities and maturity given as irrelevant inputs.

selectors.name: Correlation swap return, solve for strike
selectors.what: Return per unit notional = payoff / N = realised correlation - fixed correlation for the payer; given the return and the pairwise correlations, reverse-solve for the fixed strike.

selectors.name: Quanto option correlation risk and direction
selectors.what: A quanto lets a domestic investor swap a foreign-currency option payoff into home currency at a fixed exchange rate; the price depends on the correlation between the underlying and the exchange rate (domestic per foreign), and the more positive the correlation, the cheaper the quanto.

selectors.name: Concentration ratio and joint default
selectors.what: Concentration ratio = 1/n for n equal loans (ten equal loans: 0.1; one loan: 1); a lower ratio and a lower default correlation reduce the creditor's worst case. Joint default of two binomial events: P(X and Y) = rho x sqrt(PX(1 - PX) x PY(1 - PY)) + PX x PY, e.g. two loans with PD 10% give 10% at rho = 1, 5.5% at 0.5, 1% at 0.

maps.tested: A sleeper: the importance sheet is lukewarm on the chapter, but seven recall sources name it, several as a numerical. That divergence is itself the signal: do not deprioritise this on the strength of the sheet.
maps.specifics: Reported as '1 on correlation swap return' (numerical), 'correlation swap' (twice, separate sittings), 'swap correlation', and 'quanto options'. The correlation-swap payoff is realised average pairwise correlation minus the fixed strike, times notional. The handwritten sheet also flags concentration ratio concept and calculation from the same chapter.

maps.tested: The handwritten sheet names it as a second must-do from the correlation chapter: 'concentration ratio concept and calculation as well.'
maps.specifics: LO 8.g links correlation risk to systemic and concentration risk. The 2007-09 narrative (LO 8.b) is the case-study layer. Low recall evidence, but the sheet is specific enough that the calculation is worth one pass.

topics.vardeez: MR-8: Moderate, with the note "a) Quanto Option & Correlation Swap b) Concentration Ratio Concept & Calculation as well".

topics.title: Securitisation: Tranches, Waterfall, Prepayment and Performance Ratios

selectors.name: Delinquency ratio, plain numerical
selectors.what: Delinquency ratio = receivables overdue more than 90 days / total receivables, computed from a plain set of figures (credit-card style pool).

selectors.name: Equity cash flow after interim waterfall
selectors.what: Cash flow to the equity tranche in an interim year of the three-tranche structure: loan interest from survivors Lt = (r + s) x (N - cumulative defaults) x par, less fees and bond coupons B, with the diversion to the overcollateralisation account OCt = max[min(Lt - B, K), 0] and equity = max(Lt - B - OCt, 0).

selectors.name: Overcollateralisation account balance at year end
selectors.what: Account balance at the end of year t = (1 + r) x last year's balance + this year's diversion OCt + this year's recoveries Rt (recovery rate x defaulted par).

selectors.name: Final-year waterfall shares, senior and equity
selectors.what: Final-year funds F = grown account balance + survivors' interest and redemption at par + final-year recoveries; the senior is paid par plus final coupon first, then the mezzanine from F less the senior due, and the equity gets max(F - total bond due, 0).

selectors.name: CPR, SMM and PSA conversion
selectors.what: Converting between SMM, CPR and PSA speed: CPR = 1 - (1 - SMM)^12 and SMM = 1 - (1 - CPR)^(1/12); 100% PSA has CPR = 0.2% x month up to month 30 and a flat 6% after, and other speeds are multiples. The twist is an overcollateralised deal where the SMM denominator is the pool balance net of scheduled principal, not the note balance.

selectors.name: Prepayment rate theory and forecasting
selectors.what: Conceptual questions on prepayment measures and forecasting methodology: SMM, CPR and PSA definitions, what drives them, which asset classes they suit (mortgages, home equity, student loans; autos use absolute prepayment speed) and the effect of faster prepayment on yield and WAL.

selectors.name: Closed-book CPR, DSCR and WAL formulas
selectors.what: Direct use of the formulas CPR = 1 - (1 - SMM)^12, DSCR = net operating income / debt service, and WAL = sum of t x principal repaid in t / total principal (time in years).

selectors.name: Waterfall structure and payment order
selectors.what: The structure of a securitisation cash waterfall: cash paid top down (fees, Class A interest, A coverage tests, Class B interest, B coverage tests, and so on, equity taking the residual), with an independent agent running the tests and paying down the senior notes first when a test fails.

selectors.name: Trust versus SPV and the three SPV structures
selectors.what: Differences between issuing through a trust and through an SPV, and the three main structures: amortising (pass-through), revolving and master trust, with the asset classes and features of each.
selectors.source: Vardeez: 'Trust vs SPV'; reading note: 'LO 39.c: This can be important'

selectors.name: Effect of PD and correlation on tranches
selectors.what: How default probability and default correlation affect equity, mezzanine and senior tranches (higher PD hurts every tranche; higher correlation helps the equity and hurts the senior; the mezzanine behaves like a senior at low default rates and like equity at high ones), including the one possible calculation off the simulation.
selectors.source: Vardeez: 'Remember the impacts via the table; one calculation question possible'

selectors.name: Implied correlation
selectors.what: Definition of implied (base) correlation backed out of standard tranche prices such as the CDX tranches, how it is measured, and why it varies by tranche (correlation skew).

selectors.name: Other performance ratios: default, MPR, WAC, WAM
selectors.what: Calculating and interpreting the default ratio (written off in the period / receivables at period end), the monthly payment rate (principal and interest collections / pool balance, with a minimum as early amortisation trigger), and the balance-weighted WAC and WAM of a pool.

maps.tested: Seven sources. Split cleanly into a cash-flow computation and a structural/theory audit. One recall notes a tranche question came 'exactly the same from the mocks': a direct template-recycling flag.
maps.specifics: Reported: 'securitization: calculating cash flow into equity tranche'; 'calculate shares to senior and equity tranche'; 'securitization waterfall structure (GARP Mocks)'; 'prepayment rate (theory)'; 'CPR, SMM, PSA'; 'overcollateralisation account balance'. Closed-book: CPR = 1 - (1 - SMM)^12; DSCR = NOI / debt service; WAL = sum of t x PoolFactor. Your formula card defines overcollateralisation as funds paid less funds received.

topics.title: Altman Z-Score and Linear Discriminant Analysis

selectors.name: Direct plug: compute Z from filings
selectors.what: Compute Altman's Z from a firm's financial figures: Z = 1.2 X1 + 1.4 X2 + 3.3 X3 + 0.6 X4 + 0.999 X5, with X1 = working capital / total assets, X2 = retained earnings / total assets, X3 = EBIT / total assets, X4 = market value of equity / book value of total liabilities, X5 = sales / total assets. Also reverse-solves for one input: required ratio = (target Z - contribution of the other four) / its coefficient, then times that ratio's denominator.

selectors.name: Five ratios and weights, closed-book
selectors.what: The stem does not give the ratios or the weights: the student must recall the five ratios and their coefficients (1.2 working capital, 1.4 retained earnings, 3.3 EBIT, 0.6 market equity to liabilities, 0.999 sales, each over total assets except X4), or identify the correct ratio, weight or input among near-twin options.

selectors.name: Cut-off zones classify a firm
selectors.what: Classify a firm from its Z using the book's zones: above 3.0 unlikely to default; 2.7 to 3.0 on alert; 1.8 to 2.7 good chance of default; below 1.8 probability of a financial embarrassment very high. High Z is safe.

selectors.name: Calculate z score as discriminant function
selectors.what: Z as Altman's linear discriminant function: a fixed-weight linear combination of five accounting ratios whose cut-off values assign a firm to a group (fail or not fail); the weights were estimated to separate failed from non-failed firms in the estimation sample.

selectors.name: Trap: the two LDAs
selectors.what: The acronym LDA in a credit-scoring stem is linear discriminant analysis; in an operational risk capital stem it is the loss distribution approach (frequency and severity combined by convolution into an annual loss distribution). The trap offers the wrong meaning; the loss distribution approach itself is topic D19.

selectors.name: Borrower rating and probability of default
selectors.what: How default probability relates to credit rating: cumulative PDs rise sharply as ratings fall; for investment grade the PD in a year tends to increase with time over the first few years, while for the lowest grade it can decrease because the next year or two are critical.
selectors.source: Map #15: 'Also examinable: the relationship between borrower rating and PD (LO 27.c)'

topics.august: Altman z score - direct plug value question.

maps.tested: A pure closed-book recall item: the five component ratios and their weights are not supplied in the stem. Six sources name it; it caught candidates off guard in the 2024-25 sittings.
maps.specifics: Reported as 'Altman Z score (1)', 'Zscore', and once as 'calculate z score (LDA)', linking it to the linear discriminant analysis framing. topics.title: Liquidity-Adjusted VaR and Cost of Liquidation

selectors.name: LVaR with normal-market (constant-spread) cost
selectors.what: LVaR = VaR + cost of liquidation in a normal market, where the cost is the sum over positions of (current proportional spread x position value) / 2; includes the 'CAR, LVaR' pairing in which LVaR is asked next to capital at risk.

selectors.name: Cost of liquidation as its own number
selectors.what: The cost of liquidation alone, not added to VaR: sum of s_i x alpha_i / 2 in a normal market, or sum of (mean + lambda x sd) x alpha_i / 2 in a stressed market; the plain form of the August recall.

selectors.name: LVaR theory: spread, correlation, horizon
selectors.what: Conceptual questions on the two LVaR definitions (normal versus stressed spread), the assumption of perfect correlation of spreads across instruments, and the effect of the liquidation horizon on spread cost and market-move risk.

selectors.name: Stressed (exogenous-spread) cost of liquidation
selectors.what: Stressed cost = sum over positions of (mean spread + lambda x standard deviation of spread) x position value / 2, with lambda = 2.326 at 99% if spreads are normal; the current-spread (constant-spread) input is the sibling-swap distractor.

selectors.name: Malz expected transactions cost, 99% spread factor
selectors.what: Relative spread s = (ask - bid) / midprice; expected transactions cost = 0.5 x s x P per unit; 99% transactions cost = P x 0.5 x (s + 2.33 x sigma_s) per unit, multiplied by the units held.

selectors.name: Malz multi-day liquidation adjustment
selectors.what: LVaR over T days = one-day VaR x sqrt((1 + T)(1 + 2T) / (6T)), with T taken as the time to escape from position size against the daily trading volume (T = 5 gives 1.4832, T = 10 about 1.96).

selectors.name: Liquidity black holes and positive feedback trading
selectors.what: Why liquidity dries up when everyone wants to sell (a crowded exit) and the causes of positive feedback trading (trend trading, stop-loss rules, dynamic hedging of short option positions, synthetic options, margin calls, predatory trading); negative feedback traders stabilise, positive feedback traders destabilise.
selectors.source: Vardeez: 'Liquidity black holes and positive feedback traders'

maps.tested: Named in a pinned 'please repeat' list alongside RAROC and BCVA, and reported as an explicit numerical in at least two separate sittings. Appears in virtually every recent recall set.
maps.specifics: Reported: '1 numerical on liquidity adjusted VaR'; 'liquidity var numerical'; 'CAR, LVaR'. Two constructions must be kept apart: the constant-spread approach (add 1/2 x spread x position) and the exogenous-spread approach using the spread's own mean and volatility: stressed cost of liquidation = 0.5 x V x (mean spread + z x sd of spread). Picking the wrong one is the sibling swap.

topics.title: Incremental, Marginal and Component VaR

selectors.name: Incremental VaR of adding a position
selectors.what: Incremental VaR of including a platinum position in a silver book: the full revaluation VaR(p+a) - VaR(p), against the marginal VaR shortcut (marginal VaR x amount added). A position as large as the book needs the full revaluation.

selectors.name: Allocation using marginal VaR
selectors.what: Which position to cut or add to, or which to grow for a better return-to-risk trade-off, using marginal VaRs: cut the largest marginal VaR, add to the lowest; for return to risk, grow the position with the highest E_i / marginal VaR_i using excess returns.

selectors.name: Marginal VaR chained into Sharpe ratio
selectors.what: Given marginal VaRs, weights, volatility and the risk-free rate, back out portfolio sigma (VaR/W = sum of w_i x marginal VaR_i, sigma_p = (VaR/W)/alpha) and compute the Sharpe ratio = (expected return - rf) / sigma_p.

selectors.name: Marginal and component VaR formulas
selectors.what: Closed-book formulas: marginal VaR = (VaR/W) x beta_i; component VaR = marginal VaR x position = individual VaR x rho_i = VaR x w_i x beta_i; components sum to portfolio VaR.

selectors.name: Ranking marginal VaRs needs only beta
selectors.what: When asked to rank positions by marginal VaR (for example to choose which to cut), only the betas matter, since marginal VaR = (VaR/W) x beta_i and the factor is common to all positions.

selectors.name: Trap: marginal VaR versus component VaR
selectors.what: The stem asks for component VaR but the marginal VaR (a unitless figure, or money amount mistaken for it) or the individual VaR sits among the options, or the reverse; also the tangent (component VaR) against the curve (incremental VaR) when a position is deleted.

selectors.name: Diversified versus undiversified VaR
selectors.what: Diversified (portfolio) VaR against undiversified VaR, the sum of individual VaRs (individual VaR = alpha x sigma_i x |position|); the diversification benefit is the difference, and undiversified equals diversified only when all correlations are one with no short positions.

maps.tested: Marked Very Important by the sheet and named by five recall sources. Used both as a computation and as the input to an allocation decision.
maps.specifics: Reported: 'calculate incremental VaR of including platinum asset in the silver asset', a two-asset incremental setup; 'allocation using MVaR'; 'MVaR, vol, rf is given: calculate Sharpe ratio', which chains marginal VaR into a performance measure. Closed-book: marginal VaR = (VaR/P) x beta; component VaR = individual VaR x rho. Shortcut to find: when ranking marginal VaRs, only beta matters. The intermediate-result trap between marginal and component VaR is explicitly in GARP's repertoire.

topics.title: Lognormal VaR

selectors.name: Direct lognormal VaR from the formula
selectors.what: Plain plug-in: VaR = P x (1 - exp(muR - sigmaR x z)), with z = 1.645 at 95% and 2.326 at 99%, with mean and volatility scaled to the horizon (mu x h/250, sigma x sqrt(h/250)) where the stem gives annual figures; or reverse-solved for sigma = (muR - ln(1 - V)) / z.

selectors.name: Trap: choose between two volatilities
selectors.what: The stem gives two volatilities (16% rising to 18% six weeks ago) and the candidate must decide which regime governs the VaR horizon before applying the lognormal formula; the current 18% governs, and the old figure or an average of the two understates VaR.

selectors.name: Trap: lognormal versus normal formula
selectors.what: The lognormal form 1 - exp(mu - z x sigma), based on ln returns, must be kept distinct from the normal arithmetic form -mu + sigma x z; the normal result gives a slightly larger number and sits next to the correct answer among the options.

selectors.name: Interpret standard errors of estimators
selectors.what: Interpreting the standard error of a quantile or VaR estimate, se(q) = sqrt(p(1 - p)/n) / f(q): it falls as the sample size n rises, rises further into the tail, and gives a confidence interval q +/- 1.645 se(q) at 90%, wider for a narrower bin width, with the weaknesses of the approach.

selectors.name: Interpret QQ plots
selectors.what: Reading a quantile-quantile plot of empirical against reference quantiles: a straight line means the reference distribution fits (a different intercept and slope mean a different location and scale), steeper slopes in the tails mean heavier tails than the reference, and outliers stand out.

maps.tested: Reported as a direct-formula item, but one recall shows GARP complicating it deliberately.
maps.specifics: The complication is documented verbatim: 'a simple lognormal calculation was complicated by asking to choose between 2 volatilities, increasing from 16% to 18% six weeks ago.' That is a scope/condition trap: the candidate must decide which volatility regime governs the horizon, not just plug in. Second reported form: 'calculate lognormal VaR (direct formulae based)'. Keep the lognormal form (based on ln returns, VaR = P(1 - e^(mu - z x sigma))) distinct from the normal-arithmetic form.

selectors.name: AI vs GenAI, model groups, hallucination

topics.title: Hazard Rates, CDS Spreads and Conditional vs Unconditional PD

selectors.name: Hazard rate to cumulative and year-t PD
selectors.what: From a constant hazard rate lambda, compute survival V(t) = e^(-lambda t), cumulative PD Q(t) = 1 - e^(-lambda t), and the PD in a given year t = e^(-lambda(t-1)) - e^(-lambda t).

selectors.name: Hazard rate from PD, direct formula
selectors.what: Average hazard rate from a cumulative PD Q over T years: lambda_bar = -ln(1 - Q)/T.

selectors.name: Hazard rate from a CDS spread
selectors.what: Average hazard rate lambda_bar = s/(1 - R), with the spread s in decimals (240 bp = 0.024) and R the recovery rate; also spreads at several maturities bootstrapped into a forward hazard rate, lambda_bar(T1,T2) = (T2 x lambda_bar(T2) - T1 x lambda_bar(T1))/(T2 - T1), and the reverse from a cumulative PD to a spread, s = lambda_bar x (1 - R).

selectors.name: Marginal PD from cumulative PDs
selectors.what: Marginal (unconditional) PD in year t = C(t) - C(t-1), the difference of successive cumulative default probabilities from a table.

selectors.name: Trap: cumulative PD mistaken for hazard rate
selectors.what: 1 - e^(-lambda t) is the cumulative PD implied by a hazard rate, not the hazard rate itself; the stem or options feed a cumulative PD into s = lambda x (1 - R) as if it were lambda, or label it the hazard rate.

selectors.name: Conditional vs unconditional default probability
selectors.what: Unconditional PD in year t = C(t) - C(t-1) (as seen today); conditional PD in year t = (C(t) - C(t-1))/(1 - C(t-1)), conditional on survival to the start of the year; with a constant hazard rate the conditional PD is 1 - e^(-lambda) in every year.

topics.august: Hazard rate and PD calculation - 2Q; hazard rate from CDS spread.

maps.tested: The importance sheet calls the Estimating Default Probabilities reading the 'most important chapter' in Credit Risk and says almost all its LOs matter. Hazard rates are singled out together with marginal and conditional probability calculations.
maps.specifics: Reported: 'hazard rate calculation from PD (direct formula)'; 'hazard rate & PD'. Closed-book: lambda = spread/(1 - RR); survival = e^(-lambda x t); cumulative PD = 1 - e^(-lambda x t); marginal PD = difference of successive cumulative PDs. Correction to your formula card: it labels pd = 1 - e^(-lambda x t) as 'hazard rate'. That expression is the cumulative default probability implied by a hazard rate, not the hazard rate itself: a sibling swap waiting to happen. The conditional-vs-unconditional distinction is named by GARP-facing sources as one of the most commonly confused pairs in Part II.

topics.title: Duration Gap and Interest-Sensitive Gap

selectors.name: Duration gap, plain form
selectors.what: Leverage-adjusted duration gap DGAP = D_A - D_L x (L/A) from the asset and liability durations and the balance sheet amounts, in the plain form of the August recall.

selectors.name: Net worth impact from durations, with direction
selectors.what: Change in net worth for a given rate move: change in NW = -D_A x A x di/(1+i) + D_L x L x di/(1+i) = -DGAP x A x di/(1+i), with the direction (gain or loss) stated.

selectors.name: Liability duration that immunises net worth
selectors.what: Reverse-solve of DGAP = 0: D_L = D_A x A/L, the liability duration (or the asset duration or the A to L balance) that leaves net worth unchanged for a rate move.

selectors.name: IS gap, ISR and change in NII
selectors.what: ISGAP = ISA - ISL, relative ISGAP = ISGAP / size of institution, ISR = ISA / ISL; cumulative gap over the planning horizon and the change in net interest income: change in NII = change in i x cumulative gap.

selectors.name: Trap: polarity of the leverage-adjusted gap
selectors.what: The sign of DGAP after the leverage adjustment against a rate move: positive gap loses net worth when rates rise and gains when they fall, negative gap the reverse; D_A below D_L can still give a positive DGAP when L/A is low enough.

maps.tested: Five sources, including a reported count of two questions in one sitting. Tested as a directional impact question on net worth rather than as pure arithmetic.
maps.specifics: Reported: 'duration gap'; 'impact of asset and liability values on net worth given duration of asset and liability'; 'duration of asset liability (2)'; 'IS gap' and 'ISR gap LR'. Closed-book: change in NW = -[D_A x A - D_L x L] x change in r / (1 + r). The polarity of the leveraged-adjusted duration gap against a rate move is the single most corruptible fact here.

topics.title: Extreme Value Theory: GEV vs POT

selectors.name: GEV theory and its three cases
selectors.what: Fisher-Tippett: for iid losses the distribution of the block maximum converges to the generalised extreme value distribution, with location, scale and tail index (shape) xi. The cases are xi > 0 Frechet, xi = 0 Gumbel and xi < 0 Weibull, decided by the parent's domain of attraction.

selectors.name: GEV versus POT
selectors.what: Compares block maxima (GEV: three parameters, no threshold, can waste data because a block may hold several extremes or none) with exceedances over a high threshold (POT: two parameters, retains more tail data, needs a subjective threshold). Either approach is usually reasonable.

selectors.name: POT and the generalised Pareto
selectors.what: Peaks over threshold models the excess losses X - u over a high threshold u; by the GPBdH (Gnedenko-Pickands-Balkema-deHaan) theorem, as u gets large the excess distribution converges to the generalised Pareto, with scale beta > 0 and shape xi, pretty much regardless of the parent distribution.

selectors.name: POT threshold set too low
selectors.what: The consequence of choosing the threshold u too low: more data and lower variance but more bias, since the observations are less extreme and the GP limit applies less closely. A threshold set too high leaves too few exceedances and a higher variance.

selectors.name: Shape parameter xi > 0 means fat tails
selectors.what: A positive tail index xi means the Frechet case with heavy, power-law tails (Student t, Levy, Pareto parents), the relevant case for financial and loss data. xi = 0 is Gumbel with light exponential tails, and xi < 0 is Weibull with tails lighter than the normal.

selectors.name: Operational-risk framing of EVT
selectors.what: In operational risk the loss distribution approach is complemented by EVT for the tail: block maxima take the maximum loss per period and unit of measure (Fisher-Tippett), while POT takes the losses above a high threshold, whose excess converges to the generalised Pareto. The caution is that EVT is valid only if a single mechanism generates all observed losses, which is unlikely for pooled losses.

maps.tested: Both sheets carry the same warning: 'don't get too much into calculations here.' The comparison itself is the question.
maps.specifics: Reported: 'GEV vs POT distribution'; 'peaks over threshold'; 'POT threshold low consideration', i.e. the consequence of setting the threshold too low (more data, more bias, less 'extreme'). GEV uses block maxima and needs no threshold but wastes data; POT retains more tail observations but requires a subjective threshold. The shape parameter xi > 0 means fat tails. Also examinable: the operational-risk framing of EVT vs. block maxima, which one sheet flags as a comparison.

topics.title: Performance Measures and Attribution

selectors.name: Sharpe ratio, harder form (with M-squared)
selectors.what: Sharpe ratio = (portfolio return - risk-free rate) / sigma_P, paired with M-squared: weight w = sigma_M / sigma_P in the portfolio and T-bills, M2 = r_P* - r_M = (S_P - S_M) x sigma_M. Also asks why Sharpe is the wrong lens for one of many subportfolios (Treynor fits there).

selectors.name: Jensen's alpha and information ratio
selectors.what: Jensen's alpha = r_P - [rf + beta_P (r_M - rf)], plain or with a multifactor benchmark; information ratio = alpha / sigma(e_P), alpha per unit of residual (tracking) risk.

selectors.name: Grinold's fundamental law, maximum IR
selectors.what: Maximum attainable information ratio IR = IC x sqrt(BR), with IC the correlation of forecasts with actual returns and BR the number of independent bets; forward, or solved for IC or breadth.

selectors.name: Which measure suits which use
selectors.what: Matching Sharpe, Treynor and the information ratio to the decision context: Sharpe when the portfolio is the entire risky investment, Treynor for one subportfolio among many, the information ratio for an active portfolio mixed with the benchmark, and what sits in each denominator.

selectors.name: Sharpe ratio chained from marginal VaR
selectors.what: A Sharpe ratio calculation in which marginal VaR, volatility and the risk-free rate are given and the inputs must be chained through to the ratio: Sharpe = (return - rf) / sigma.

selectors.name: Attribution: allocation and selection effects
selectors.what: Performance attribution against the bogey: asset allocation = sum of (w_P - w_B) x r_index; security selection = sum of w_P x (r_P - r_index); together they equal the excess return. Within a class, sector allocation plus security selection is multiplied by the class weight before entering the total.

selectors.name: Time-weighted versus dollar-weighted return
selectors.what: Distinguishing the time-weighted (geometric, equal weight per period) return from the dollar-weighted return (IRR of the cash flows), which one judges the manager and which reflects the client's experience, and computing them from a short cash-flow example.

selectors.name: Style analysis
selectors.what: Sharpe's style analysis: regressing fund returns on asset-class indexes with non-negative coefficients summing to 100%; reading the weights as the style mix, R-squared as the share of variability explained by style, and the intercept as the average return from security selection.
selectors.source: Vardeez: 'Style analysis' (IM-7 e, IM-3 f; 'the last LO in this chapter')

topics.title: Non-Parametric VaR: Weighted HS, Bootstrap and FHS

selectors.name: Age-weighted HS (BRW) weights and VaR
selectors.what: Boudoukh-Richardson-Whitelaw weights: w(1) = (1 - lambda)/(1 - lambda^n), w(i) = lambda^(i-1) x w(1), cumulative weight on the k most recent observations = (1 - lambda^k)/(1 - lambda^n). Rank the P/L from the worst loss, accumulate the weights and read the VaR where the cumulative weight reaches 1 - alpha (interpolation allowed).

selectors.name: Volatility-weighted HS (HW), polarity
selectors.what: Hull-White adjusted return r*(t,i) = r(t,i) x sigma(T,i)/sigma(t,i), the current volatility forecast over the forecast for day t; returns are scaled up when current volatility is above the volatility on the day observed and down when it is below, then VaR or ES is taken the equal-weight way. The reversed statement and the inverted ratio are the distractors.

selectors.name: Bootstrap HS property question
selectors.what: A property or statement question on bootstrapped historical simulation: resampling the data with replacement, one VaR or ES per resample (resample ES is the average of the losses exceeding the resample VaR), the best estimate being the mean of the resample estimates, use for precision and confidence intervals (percentile, BCa), the assumption of independence over time, and that the bootstrap cannot give a VaR above the largest historical loss.

selectors.name: Differences among the non-parametric approaches
selectors.what: Compares or contrasts basic HS, bootstrap, age-weighted, volatility-weighted, correlation-weighted and filtered HS, and their advantages and disadvantages: what each adjusts (age, volatility, correlation, standardised returns), which can exceed the largest historical loss, dependence on the data window and ghost effects.

selectors.name: Expected shortfall in filtered HS
selectors.what: Filtered historical simulation (Barone-Adesi et al.): fit an asymmetric GARCH, divide realised returns by their volatility forecasts to get iid standardised returns, bootstrap them, multiply by tomorrow's volatility forecast, then take VaR or ES (the average of the simulated losses beyond VaR). Tests that FHS extends easily to ES, that VaR and ES can exceed the largest historical loss, and that whole standardised vectors are bootstrapped for a multi-asset portfolio.

maps.tested: A four-way sibling set (age-weighted, volatility-weighted, correlation-weighted, filtered), which is exactly the structure GARP builds four-statement audits from.
maps.specifics: Reported: 'bootstrap HS property question'; 'difference in non-parametric approaches'; 'expected shortfall in filtered historical simulation'. The polarity trap is documented in GARP's own materials: volatility-weighted HS adjusts historical returns upward when current volatility is above the historical level; the reversed version is the distractor.

topics.title: Wrong-Way and Right-Way Risk

selectors.name: Classify trades as wrong-way or right-way
selectors.what: Given a trade and a counterparty, say whether it is wrong-way or right-way risk: put options on a stock correlated with the counterparty, FX forwards and cross-currency swaps with a sovereign paid in its local currency, receiver or payer interest rate swaps, commodity swaps hedged by a producer, and CDS where the reference entity is linked to the counterparty (buyer wrong-way, seller right-way).

selectors.name: Test for wrong-way risk
selectors.what: The test itself: wrong-way risk is an unfavourable dependence between exposure and counterparty credit quality, so ask what makes the exposure rise and whether the same event weakens the counterparty; right-way risk is the favourable dependence and reduces CVA. Includes general versus specific WWR, and that WWR increases (not decreases) with counterparty credit quality.

selectors.name: Wrong-way collateral and margin
selectors.what: Which collateral is wrong-way (a government bond securing a payer swap, cash in the currency being paid on a cross-currency swap, an entity's own bonds, a bank's own sovereign bonds) and how collateral affects WWR: margin helps if exposure builds gradually before default and is near useless if exposure jumps at default; it reduces but does not eliminate WWR.

selectors.name: Effect of wrong-way risk on CCPs
selectors.what: Why CCPs are prone to WWR: they rely on variation and initial margin (especially clearing CDSs), initial margin and default fund contributions follow market risk and so implicitly ignore WWR, and the defaulter-pays resources may be insufficient, loading losses on surviving members and possibly the CCP itself.

selectors.name: Wrong-way modelling approaches
selectors.what: Match each approach to its features: hazard rate (intensity) with stochastic spreads, tractable but weak dependence; structural with a bivariate copula, strong effect but opaque correlation; parametric (Hull and White) with a functional link of default probability to exposure; jump, with the FX rate jumping at default, suited to specific WWR.

maps.specifics: Reported verbatim: 'RWR & WWR (2 theory questions): confusing, study...'. The formula card frames it correctly as 'identify if there is any correlation'. topics.title: Collateral, Two-Way CSA, Margin Period of Risk and Netting

selectors.name: Two-way vs one-way CSA, rating-linked terms
selectors.what: Differences between no CSA, a one-way CSA (only one party receives; infinite threshold for the other) and a two-way CSA (both post; typical of financial counterparties, zero thresholds standard interbank), and how threshold, initial margin and MTA are linked to credit quality (rating-linked parameters) with their problems (slow ratings, liquidity cliff effects).

selectors.name: Margin period of risk and collateralised CVA
selectors.what: MPoR as the effective time from the counterparty ceasing to post margin until all trades are closed out and replaced, its pre-default and post-default components, typical values (Basel II 10 business days, longer for large or illiquid portfolios and disputes, CCPs about 5 days) and its effect on collateralised exposure and CVA: with variation margin only, risk falls by about sqrt(maturity / MPoR) and CVA_coll = CVA_uncoll / reduction factor, with maturity and MPoR in the same units.

selectors.name: Collateral required: threshold, MTA, rounding
selectors.what: Credit support amount (margin to call or post) from the netted MtM value, the threshold(s), MTA, rounding and the margin already held: CSA amount = max(value - K_C, 0) - max(-value - K_P, 0) - C, where K_C is the counterparty's threshold, K_P the calculating party's own threshold and C the credit support balance (negative if posted). Positive means call or request return, negative means post or return.

selectors.name: Trap: threshold plus MTA fails, no call
selectors.what: Full data is supplied but the required amount after threshold and balance is below the MTA, so no transfer is made and the correct answer is zero. Once the MTA is passed the full amount moves: the MTA is not deducted from the amount due.

selectors.name: Overcollateralisation: initial margin and haircuts
selectors.what: Initial margin (independent amount, a negative threshold) and haircuts as sources of overcollateralisation: required margin = max(value - K_C, 0) + initial margin; with a haircut h, value credited = (1 - h) x market value, so to deliver credit X post X / (1 - h). The securitisation overcollateralisation account is drilled in A9.

selectors.name: Features and terms of a collateral agreement
selectors.what: Features of the CSA under the ISDA Master Agreement, CR-17 g: valuation method and timing, margin amount, transfer mechanics, eligible margin, substitutions, dispute resolution, remuneration, initial margin, haircuts, rehypothecation, triggers, and how threshold, MTA and rounding work; terms fixed at signing and changed only by mutual amendment.

selectors.name: Disputes and reconciliation
selectors.what: CR-17 f: the valuation agent (normally the party calling for margin), why collateral disputes arise (trade population, valuation methodology, application of CSA rules, market data and close time, valuation of posted collateral) and how reconciliation of portfolios and margin requirements resolves them; frequency of reconciliation and the effect on capital.

selectors.name: Risks created by collateralisation, role misassignment
selectors.what: CR-17 j: how market (including FX and wrong-way margin), operational and liquidity risk, including funding liquidity risk, arise through margin, and which party bears each: liquidation risk sits with the margin holder, funding liquidity risk with the party that must post, and a one-way CSA hurts the margin giver.

selectors.name: Termination features and trade compression
selectors.what: CR-16 d: mandatory, optional and contingent break clauses and Additional Termination Events (rating downgrade) with their benefits and dangers (cliff-edge effects, no Basel capital relief for rating triggers); trade compression as multilateral tear-up of redundant trades that cuts gross notional but not market risk, including finding the net notional and the party holding the net position.

topics.title: Three Lines of Defence and Operational Risk Governance

selectors.name: Three lines: who does what
selectors.what: Who owns and who does what in the three lines of operational risk management: risk owners in the business (line 1, with risk champions at 1.5), the independent corporate risk function (line 2, owns the methodology, challenges, may veto), internal audit (line 3, independent assurance). Each wrong option moves an activity across a line, for example the risk function owning the risk, the first line not signing off its own assessment, or internal audit relying only on the risk function's testing.

selectors.name: Basel event-type taxonomy, Levels 1 to 3
selectors.what: Classify an operational loss event into the seven Basel Level 1 event types and their Level 2 categories, or recognise the Level 3 examples that discriminate (insider trading on or not on the firm's account, check kiting by internal or external party, model error versus model misoperation, utility outage, hacking). Level 3 gives examples only; the regulatory categories are Levels 1 and 2.

selectors.name: Board, committees, risk appetite ownership
selectors.what: Who does what among the board, the board risk committee, the executive and group operational risk committees and senior management: the board is ultimately responsible, approves the framework and the risk appetite statement and owns the limits, committees escalate upward and recommend, senior management implements. Also what makes a risk appetite statement and a risk culture sound.

maps.specifics: Reported: 'three lines of Operational Risk Management'; 'Ops Risk Level 3 categorisation': the Basel event-type taxonomy at its third level, a separate recall item. selectors.name: Hedge fund risks, systemic risk, regulation, structure

topics.title: Gauss+ and Vasicek

selectors.name: Gauss+ factor changes, plain form
selectors.what: The change in one Gauss+ factor over dt from given inputs: dr = -alpha_r (r - m) dt with no shock; dm = -alpha_m (m - l) dt plus a shock of standard deviation sigma_m x sqrt(dt); dl = -alpha_l (l - mu) dt plus a shock of standard deviation sigma_l x sqrt(dt).

selectors.name: Expected rate in T years, theta built
selectors.what: Closed-book E[r_T] = r0 e^(-kT) + theta(1 - e^(-kT)), where theta = r_inf + lambda/k is built from the real-world long-run rate and the risk premium before it is used.

selectors.name: Half-life ln 2 / k
selectors.what: Half-life h = ln 2 / k: the time to cover half the distance between the current rate and theta. Forward, or solved for k from a stated half-life; also the half-lives of the Gauss+ factors (ln 2 / alpha).

selectors.name: Vasicek rate change and standard deviation
selectors.what: Over a short step dt: expected change = k(theta - r) dt and standard deviation = sigma x sqrt(dt); also the terminal standard deviation after T years, sigma x sqrt((1 - e^(-2kT)) / (2k)).

selectors.name: LO 14.g expected rate in T years
selectors.what: Plug-in of the given r0, k, theta and horizon T (for instance 7 years) into E[r_T] = r0 e^(-kT) + theta(1 - e^(-kT)), with theta stated directly.

selectors.name: Gauss+ structure: cascade, no shock on r
selectors.what: The Gauss+ structure and how it compares with Vasicek: the short rate r reverts to the medium-term factor m, m reverts to the long-term factor l, l reverts to the constant mu; no random shock on r; three factors but only two sources of risk (dW1, dW2); the implications for matching the hump-shaped term structure of volatility.

maps.tested: Reading 16 is flagged as a new chapter, highly testable: new readings are disproportionately sampled.
maps.specifics: Closed-book: E[r_T] = r0 e^(-kT) + theta(1 - e^(-kT)); half-life = ln 2 / k. The sheet says 'Vasicek model calculation can come' and separately flags LO 14.g (expected rate in T years). The Gauss+ multi-factor structure is the genuinely new material.

topics.title: Monitoring Liquidity: TSECF, TSAA and Liquidity Stress Testing

selectors.name: TSECF and TSAA numerical
selectors.what: Given a purchase, sale or other transaction, say which term structures (TSECF, TSAA, TSLGC) move and by how much: a purchase puts the dirty-price outflow, coupons and redemption in the TSECF and raises the TSAA until expiry.

selectors.name: Trend, seasonal, cyclical liquidity requirement
selectors.what: Forecast deposits and loans as trend + seasonal + cyclical (cyclical = last year's actual - last year's trend-plus-seasonal for that week), then the estimated liquidity deficit (-) or surplus (+) = change in deposits - change in loans.

selectors.name: Repo of an available asset
selectors.what: Cash raised by repoing a bond = N x (Price% + c x tau) x (1 - h), placed in the TSCLGC, with the haircut and the accrued interest since the last coupon; the repayment at maturity = cash x (1 + r_repo x term).

selectors.name: TSECCF with initial cash, asset sale
selectors.what: Cumulate the TSECF from Cash(t0) to get the TSECCF, find its most negative point, and size the asset sale that keeps TSLe = TSECCF + TSCLGC non-negative: minimum notional = |most negative TSECCF| / expected price.

selectors.name: Deterministic versus stochastic cash flows
selectors.what: Classify a cash flow by whether its amount and its time are deterministic or stochastic, with examples such as coupons of risk-free fixed-rate bonds, one-touch option payouts, indexed, credit-related, behavioural and new-business flows.

selectors.name: Liquidity options
selectors.what: Identify liquidity options (committed credit lines, sight and savings deposits, prepayable fixed-rate loans) and their liquidity impact and financial impact on the bank, and which of the two can be hedged.

selectors.name: Contingent liquidity and liquid asset buffer
selectors.what: Stressed liquid asset buffer = liquid asset buffer - stressed outflows + stressed inflows, with inflows possibly capped (for example at 75% of outflows under the LCR).
selectors.source: Vardeez: 'Contingent liquidity via liquid asset buffer: calculation important'

selectors.name: Types of liquidity risk reports
selectors.what: Recognise and interpret the liquidity reports: deposit tracker (loan-to-deposit ratio against a board limit), daily liquidity report, funding maturity gap, funding concentration against a limit, undrawn commitments, and the cash flow survival report.
selectors.source: Vardeez: 'Know the different liquidity reports; basics and interpretation only'

topics.title: Non-Deposit Liabilities, Pooled Cost of Funds and Liquidity Transfer Pricing

selectors.name: Non-deposit sources and choosing among them
selectors.what: Distinguishes the sources of non-deposit liabilities (Fed funds, repurchase agreements, discount window and FHLB advances, negotiable CDs, Eurocurrency deposits, commercial paper, capital notes and debentures) and the five factors in choosing a source: relative cost, risk, length of time needed, size of the borrower and regulations.

selectors.name: Pooled-funds against historical average cost
selectors.what: Overall cost of funds by the two Rose and Hudgins approaches. Historical average: weighted average interest expense = interest paid / total funds raised; break-even rate = (interest + other operating costs) / earning assets; overall cost of capital = break-even + [after-tax equity cost / (1 - t)] x (equity / earning assets). Pooled-funds (forward looking): pooled expense = all expected operating expenses / all new funds; hurdle rate = all expected operating costs / dollars placed in earning assets. Also the effective cost rate of one source, (interest + noninterest access costs) / net investable funds.

selectors.name: Pooled average cost against matched-maturity marginal cost
selectors.what: Compares the LTP approaches (zero cost, pooled average cost, matched-maturity marginal cost) and charges a loan by term: premium by maturity against a flat average, blended premium for a linearly amortising loan = sum(t x TLP) / sum(t), behavioural maturity for mortgages, larger credits for sticky deposits.

selectors.name: LTP charging liquidity cost back to business lines
selectors.what: What LTP is and the better-practice governance for it: charges users of funds, credits providers of funds, and recoups the cost of the liquidity cushion from contingent commitments by predicted use, e.g. contingent charge = (limit - drawn) / limit x likelihood of drawdown x cost of funding the cushion.

selectors.name: Available funds gap
selectors.what: Available funds gap = (current and projected loans and investments desired) - (current and expected deposit inflows and other available funds), the amount to be raised from non-deposit sources, usually with a small cushion added.

maps.tested: Reported once in a consolidated list; rated Important by the sheet.
maps.specifics: Reported: 'pooled cost approach, etc.' The examinable contrast is the pooled-funds-cost approach against the marginal-cost and historical-average-cost approaches for pricing deposits and non-deposit liabilities. LTP's role in charging liquidity cost back to business lines is the governance angle.

topics.title: Private Credit, Private Markets and Their Drivers

selectors.name: Private credit growth drivers, BIS regression
selectors.what: The four drivers of private credit growth (low policy rates, low banking-sector efficiency measured by the FI index, higher bank regulatory stringency, rising corporate leverage) and how the BIS regression (45 countries, 2010 to 2019, new private credit origination) ranks them by economic effect: FI index decline about +33%, policy rate decline about +12%, regulatory stringency rise about +2% to 4%, corporate leverage under 1%.

selectors.name: Bank disintermediation, private credit vs bank loans
selectors.what: Why banks retreated after 2007 to 2009 and private credit funds took over lending to riskier mid-sized firms, and how private credit loans compare with bank loans (flexible terms, tailored covenants, fast execution). The cost of equity, cost of debt and leverage story for US banks vs BDCs: BDC cost of equity below banks', cost of debt marginally above, banks' funding advantage narrowed by about 250 bp in 2010 to 2019, equally from higher bank cost of equity and BDC leverage, with cost of debt playing almost no role.

selectors.name: Valuation opacity, stale marks, NAV metrics
selectors.what: Why private credit valuations are opaque (few comparables, infrequent valuations, no secondary market, no mandated method) and what follows: stale marks overstate value and returns, inflate manager fees, and defer and then bunch losses; NAV can differ from price for several quarters; more frequent valuation is not automatically better.

selectors.name: Financial-stability concerns and IMF policy fixes
selectors.what: The IMF's assessment of private credit risks to financial stability (credit, liquidity, leverage, interconnectedness, conduct, underwriting; judged moderate today but untested by a serious downturn) and the matching policy recommendations (bank-like monitoring, closed-end structures and liquidity tools, leverage reporting and stress tests, valuation oversight, data sharing, conflict disclosure).

selectors.name: PE performance: IRR, TVPI, DPI, PME
selectors.what: Compute or compare the private equity performance measures: DPI = distributions / paid-in, RVPI = residual value (NAV) / paid-in, TVPI = DPI + RVPI, IRR as the rate solving the sum of cash flows over (1 + r)^t = 0 (calls negative, distributions positive), and PME as the sum of distributions discounted at index returns over the sum of calls discounted at index returns (above 1 means the fund outperformed the index). Also which measure is least manipulable, and the advantages and weaknesses of each.

selectors.name: Private markets structures, co-investing, intermediated vehicles

topics.title: Asset vs Borrowed Liquidity Management and the Investment Function

selectors.name: Asset vs borrowed vs balanced liquidity

selectors.name: Net liquidity position as the starting point
selectors.what: Net liquidity position Lt = supplies (deposit inflows, nondeposit service revenues, loan repayments, asset sales, money market borrowings) - demands (withdrawals, acceptable loan requests, repaid borrowings, operating expenses, dividends). selectors.what: Capital (or RWA) for one corporate loan under Advanced IRB: WCDR = N((N^-1(PD) + sqrt(rho) x N^-1(0.999)) / sqrt(1 - rho)), with the wholesale correlation rho (0.12 to 0.24, falling as PD rises); Capital = EAD x LGD x (WCDR - PD) x MA; RWA = 12.5 x capital; MA from the maturity formula when M is given.

selectors.name: Retail IRB, fixed correlation, RWA
selectors.what: Capital or RWA for a retail exposure: the same WCDR formula with the fixed retail correlation (0.15 residential mortgages, 0.04 qualifying revolving, 0.03 to 0.16 formula for other retail) and no maturity adjustment, reported as RWA = 12.5 x EAD x LGD x (DR - PD).

selectors.name: Foundation versus Advanced IRB inputs
selectors.what: Which inputs the bank estimates and which the supervisor sets: Foundation IRB bank supplies PD only, with supervisory EAD, LGD (45% senior, 75% subordinated) and MA of 2.5, and a PD floor of 0.0003 for bank and corporate exposures; Advanced IRB bank supplies PD, LGD, EAD and MA; also the Basel II standardized approach and why IRB was expected to suit large banks.

selectors.name: December 2017 IRB revisions
selectors.what: What the December 2017 reforms changed in IRB: A-IRB removed for large and mid-sized corporates (revenues above EUR 500 million) and for banks and other financial institutions (to F-IRB or SA), all IRB removed for equities, input floors (PD floors under both approaches, LGD and EAD floors under A-IRB only), F-IRB senior unsecured LGD cut from 45% to 40%, the 1.06 scaling factor removed; also the motivation (restore credibility and comparability of RWAs).

selectors.name: The 72.5% output floor
selectors.what: RWA = max(RWA under approved approaches, 72.5% x RWA under the standardised approaches only); how the floor binds against modelled RWA, the approaches included in the floor base, the phase-in to 72.5% by 1 January 2027, and how input floors and the output floor differ.

topics.title: Net Stable Funding Ratio, LCR and Leverage Ratio

selectors.name: NSFR from ASF and RSF factors
selectors.what: NSFR = ASF / RSF, where ASF = sum of (liability or equity amount x ASF factor) and RSF = sum of (asset amount x RSF factor), from a balance sheet with the factors given; compliant when at least 1.

selectors.name: NSFR shortfall: new funding needed
selectors.what: The amount of new funding needed to bring NSFR to 100%, counting both legs: the funding adds ASF and its deployment into an asset adds RSF, so ASF + a x X = RSF + r x X and X = (RSF - ASF) / (a - r).

selectors.name: NSFR versus LCR: pick the right factors
selectors.what: A table gives both parameter sets (ASF and RSF factors for the NSFR; HQLA factors and run-off rates for the LCR); the question asks for NSFR = ASF / RSF or LCR = HQLA / net cash outflows over 30 days, and the right factors must be taken for the ratio asked.

selectors.name: Leverage ratio calculation
selectors.what: Leverage ratio = Core Tier 1 capital / Leverage Exposure, at least 3%, with the exposure including on-balance-sheet assets and fractions of off-balance-sheet items; also the G-SIB leverage buffer of 50% of the risk-weighted G-SIB higher-loss absorbency requirement, met with Tier 1 capital.
